title: Bathinda cotton ginning & pressing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A ginning and pressing unit buys seed cotton (kapas) at the mandi, separates lint from seed, bales and presses it, and sells lint to spinning mills and seed to oil extractors. **Cash is made on the spread between kapas purchase and lint sale, not on volume alone.** The ginner's real asset is the bale in the godown and the mill's order; the real risk is holding that bale while the price moves. Ginning is inherently low value-adding and fragmented with low entry barriers, so pricing power sits with the mill buyer, not the ginner [9][11]. ## Where value and cash sit now
Arrivals in north India have slowed and spinners are buying more, tightening the market [1][2][3]. **That is good for a ginner who already holds stock and bad for one who must buy kapas at today's higher price to fill an old-priced order.** Peer results show the trap: AB Cotspin's Q1 FY27 revenue rose 52.94% to Rs 102.01 crore while operating margin fell to 12.90% from 22.29% [4][5]. So when a proposal lands, check whether the sales growth is backed by a matching purchase contract; if the margin is thinner than last year, ask what price the lint is already sold at. ## The growth opportunity to pursue
Punjab GST collections rose 9.7% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1% [D], and India-wide cotton textile output (NIC 13) is up 13.1% YoY [D]. **Pursue ginners tied to spinning mills with confirmed offtake, and integrated units with captive ginning and oil extraction** — the ICRA case shows location near cotton-growing areas and vertical integration support the rating [8]. Reputed, geographically spread clientele (Vardhman-type buyers) is a genuine strength [10]. Avoid pure traders with no ginning asset and units whose book is one large unhedged position. ## How to grow safely
Structure against stock, not against hope. **Take a monthly stock-and-receivables statement, a godown inspection and the sales register every month**, and reconcile bales pledged to bales in the godown. Keep drawing power tied to insured, quality-graded stock. Ask for the mill purchase contract behind each large order. Note that bank credit is growing 15.2% YoY against output of 11.9% [D] — money is chasing this trade, so your edge is discipline, not speed. ## Early-warning signs
- **Bale holding period lengthening beyond the normal cycle** — collect from customer the current days-of-stock; if it stretches, ask why the mill lifted slower. - **Margin compression with rising revenue** — the AB Cotspin pattern [4]; ask for the sale price locked per bale. - **Rising reliance on external borrowing for working capital** — the Harekrushna Cottex weakness [11]; ask for the debt-to-stock ratio. - **Client concentration** — if one mill is over half of sales, ask for the contract and payment history. - **Old rating reports**: the S.S. Sources say little specifically about Bathinda, so lean on first principles and these peers.

One buyer over half of sales -> cap exposure and seek contract
